headings.title: Introduction to Accessory Male Reproductive Organs
headings.content: The male reproductive system relies on more than just the primary organs that produce sperm. The accessory male reproductive organs are a collection of glands and tubes that produce the fluid medium essential for nourishing, transporting, and protecting sperm cells. Without these vital secretions, sperm cannot survive long in the acidic environment of the female reproductive tract, let alone swim effectively toward an egg. Together, the seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands contribute the liquid portion of semen, transforming plain sperm cells into a functional reproductive fluid.

headings.title: Anatomy and Secretory Role of the Seminal Vesicles
headings.content:
Positioned at the base of the bladder, the seminal vesicles are a pair of pouch-like glands that contribute the largest volume—about 60%—to total semen production. Their fluid is thick, yellowish, and packed with substances designed to fuel sperm. 

- **Fructose**: A simple sugar that provides the main energy source for sperm motility.
- **Prostaglandins**: Chemicals that help stimulate smooth muscle contractions in the female reproductive tract to help move sperm upward.
- **Clotting proteins**: Factors that temporarily thicken semen after ejaculation so it stays inside the vaginal canal.

headings.title: Structure and Function of the Prostate Gland
headings.content: The prostate is a walnut-sized, single gland situated directly beneath the urinary bladder, wrapping entirely around the first portion of the urethra. It secretes a milky, slightly acidic fluid that makes up roughly 30% of semen volume. This fluid contains citric acid for nutrient use, various enzymes, and **prostate-specific antigen (PSA)**, which helps liquefy semen shortly after clotting so sperm can swim freely. Because of its anatomical position surrounding the urethra, any enlargement of the prostate directly interferes with normal urination.

headings.title: Bulbourethral Glands (Cowper's Glands) and Lubrication
headings.content: Located inferior to the prostate gland, the pea-sized bulbourethral glands secrete a clear, slippery, alkaline mucus into the spongy urethra just before ejaculation. This mucus serves a dual defensive and functional role. First, it neutralizes any residual acidic traces of urine lingering inside the urethra, shielding fragile sperm cells from chemical damage. Second, it acts as a primary lubricant for the tip of the penis during sexual arousal. Students often confuse this clear pre-ejaculatory fluid with semen itself, though it contains little to no actual sperm.

headings.title: Composition and Physiological Importance of Semen
headings.content:
Semen is a complex mixture of sperm from the testes and liquid secretions from all three accessory glands. Its overall pH is mildly alkaline, usually ranging between 7.2 and 7.8, which counteracts the naturally acidic environment of the female vagina. 

| Gland Source | Contribution to Semen | Key Secretion Components |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Seminal Vesicles | ~60% | Fructose, prostaglandins, clotting proteins |
| Prostate Gland | ~30% | Citric acid, enzymes, PSA |
| Bulbourethral Glands | <5% | Alkaline mucus, lubricants |
| Testes | ~5% | Spermatozoa |

Beyond simple transport, semen delivers antibacterial agents and local immune suppressants to help protect sperm during their journey.

headings.title: Endocrine Control and Hormonal Regulation
headings.content: The growth, maintenance, and secretory activity of the male accessory reproductive organs depend heavily on androgens, primarily **testosterone**. Produced mainly by the interstitial cells of the testes under the command of pituitary hormones (LH and FSH), testosterone prompts these glands to develop fully during puberty and maintain their function throughout adulthood. If testosterone levels drop significantly, the seminal vesicles and prostate can undergo shrinkage and a sharp decrease in fluid output, directly impairing male fertility.

headings.title: Clinical Conditions Affecting Male Accessory Organs
headings.content: The accessory reproductive organs are frequent sites of common clinical disorders, especially as men age. **Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)** involves non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate, squeezing the urethra and causing urinary frequency or weak flow. **Prostatitis**, an inflammation or bacterial infection of the prostate, causes pelvic pain and painful urination. Additionally, prostate cancer is one of the most common malignancies in older men, often screened for using blood tests that measure prostate-specific antigen levels and digital rectal examinations.
